title: Redwood cost/econ discovery with Lighthouse Capital
summary: Discovery focused on per-token economics and levers to control unit costs across Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. Customer provided traffic profile and budget constraints; agreed next steps for pricing sheet, benchmarking data, and a pilot proposal.
topics: hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs

Priya to share batching/caching benchmark spreadsheet and recommended config (by 2026-07-22)
Schedule 1-hour technical deep dive with Samantha for infra specifics (target week of 2026-07-27)

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-19
Time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Mark (CTO - Lighthouse), Emily (Head of ML), Samantha (Infra)

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone thanks for joining, uh this is Jordan from Redwood, I'll kick us off. Priya our SE is here, she'll go deep on the cost levers. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Mark: Good thanks, Mark here. We're excited to understand the economics — Emily wanted this to be focused on cost/unit and what controls we have.
[00:16] Emily: Yeah hi, quick context: prototypes run against hosted endpoints but costs spiked when we increased seq length. We have a monthly budget range we'd like to keep the pilot in, around 25k a month.
[00:27] Priya: Great, that's super helpful. We usually break this down into per-token hosted pricing, then batching/caching and quantization as levers. Also Dedicated and Private change the unit economics — predictable throughput vs lower per-token op costs.
[00:36] Jordan: Quick agenda: we'll ask a few qualification q's, Priya will go through the rough math and tradeoffs, and we'll propose next steps for a pilot.
[00:44] Mark: Sounds good.

[01:12] Priya: Can you share current traffic profile? what's your qps, average token length, and p95 latency target?
[01:18] Samantha: Right now peak qps is about 45, avg prompt+response about 600 tokens, but there are heavy tails — 5-10% of calls exceed 2k tokens. We need p95 under 400ms for interactive UI.
[01:31] Priya: Excellent. So quick sanity math: if you do 45 qps sustained, that's about 3.9M requests/day — but I assume that peak is bursts, not 24/7?
[01:40] Samantha: Correct, it's bursty during market hours, sustained baseline maybe 6-8 qps.

[02:05] Priya: Ok, for cost modeling we use tokens/month. For example, hosted per-token list pricing (example numbers) — say $0.002 per 1k prompt tokens and $0.006 per 1k completion tokens — these are illustrative; exact tiers depend on model size. So if average call is 600 tokens with 200 prompt / 400 completion, that's ~0.2 request dollars? sorry, math: that's about 0.36 cents per request, translates to about ~360k requests per $1k? The point is you can multiply tokens/month by per-1k rate.
[02:42] Mark: Wait can you repeat the per-token framing — we bill per 1k tokens? And is that split prompt vs completion?
[02:48] Jordan: Yes typically per-1k tokens, and some models or plans differentiate prompt vs completion, although we often just show blended per-token for simplicity.
[02:56] Emily: Are these rates public? How do dedicated rates compare?
[03:01] Priya: Hosted list numbers are public but enterprise deals have discounts. Dedicated moves from per-token to more capacity/throughput pricing — you reserve GPU pools and either get lower effective per-token compute cost or fixed monthly. For example, a dedicated pod could be priced such that for heavy throughput workloads your effective per-token cost drops by 30-60% relative to hosted, depending on utilization and model.
[03:27] Samantha: How much utilization do we need to realize that? We won't be at 100% obviously.
[03:31] Priya: With dedicated you get predictable slots; the math depends on average sequence length distribution and batching. At 60-70% utilization you start to see the good cost benefits; at lower utilization the fixed cost amortization hurts. We can run a utilization simulation if you provide traffic histograms.

[04:05] Mark: What's the role of batching here? We assumed batching just increases latency but reduces cost. How does Redwood handle batching for interactive apps?
[04:13] Priya: Good q — Redwood uses continuous batching with latency SLOs. For interactive p95 400ms target, we do micro-batches and prioritize by latency. Batching reduces per-token kernel overhead and amortizes expensive attention compute, lowering cost per token. But if you need strict tail latency, batching window shrinks and the cost benefit reduces. There's a sweet spot — e.g., a 20-50ms additional queuing can yield significant cost reductions for high qps workloads.
[04:42] Emily: And KV caching? We expect many repeated prefixes in our use case.
[04:47] Priya: KV (K-V) cache is huge for cost; prefix caching keeps the past key/values so repeated prompts (or similar warm prefixes) avoid re-compute. We have auto prefix caching and suggestions to instrument cache hit rates. If you can get a 30-40% cache hit on common flows, your token compute goes down linearly with hits. Note caveat: cacheable patterns depend on prompt design.

[05:20] Jordan: To anchor with numbers: if you have 1M tokens/month and a hosted blended rate of $0.01 per 1k tokens (example), that's $10/month. If caching reduces tokens served by 30%, you save $3. So scale that to your volumes.
[05:36] Mark: Can you show an example with our expected pilot budget? $25k/month — what kind of QPS and latency can we expect?
[05:43] Priya: Rough back of envelope — if average call is 600 tokens, 1M calls is 600M tokens. At hosted $0.01 per 1k that's $6k. For 25k budget, that's ~4.16B tokens/month. Divide by 600 tokens/call equals ~6.9M calls/month, about 80 calls/sec sustained. But again that's simplistic — you need to factor in completion vs prompt split and discounts.
[06:10] Emily: Those numbers help. We're also very interested in quantized model variants — can that reduce token cost?
[06:16] Priya: Quantization reduces memory and can increase throughput; if a quantized model runs 20-40% faster on a given GPU, that translates into lower per-token runtime cost. However quality/regression checks required. We do model-side recommendations: Q4bit/8bit, dynamic range quantization, etc.
[06:34] Samantha: And how does private/VPC change pricing? If we run Private on our cloud or on-prem we still pay Redwood for software and maybe a base infra fee?
[06:42] Jordan: For Private you generally have a licensing/seat and infrastructure fee, and we support bring-your-own instances or we can manage infra. The per-token compute is essentially the infra cost + software fee; customers with capacity and strict data residency often prefer private even if capex is higher because of control.

[07:12] Mark: Security: we need SOC 2 and audit logs, SSO — is that available across hosted and dedicated?
[07:18] Jordan: Yes Hosted enterprise plans and Dedicated/Private have SOC 2, SSO (SAML), RBAC, KMS integrations, and audit logs. We'll share our security docs.

[07:40] Priya: Back to economics — a common approach for customers is a 3-month pilot on Hosted with sample traffic and instrumentation: we gather cache hit rates, batching gains, and then run a simulation for Dedicated. That gives an apples-to-apples comparison and quantifies break-even utilization.
[07:56] Emily: That seems reasonable; we can instrument quickly.

[08:10] Mark: Any gotchas on billing e.g., retries, hot-looping bots that inflate token counts?
[08:15] Jordan: We recommend rate-limiting and dedupe at application layer; on our side we report token drains and per-route usage. Retries and rapid polling will obviously balloon token usage — we'll flag anomalous patterns with alerts if enabled.

[08:37] Priya: Also think about model variants: cheaper smaller models for certain flows (summarization vs deep reasoning) — routing policy can send cheaper models for low-sensitivity calls. That reduces effective blended rate.

[09:02] Emily: For our pilot, can Redwood help set up routing rules and a cost dashboard?
[09:07] Jordan: Yes we include per-route dashboards and cost breakdowns; we'll provide a template dashboard for your use case.

[09:30] 
-- transcript jumps, some crosstalk --
[09:48] Samantha: Our infra question: can Redwood Dedicated be hosted in our cloud region in us-west-2? We need data residency.
[09:55] Priya: Yes, Dedicated can be provisioned in specific cloud regions; Private is preferred if you need VPC peering and strict network controls.

[10:12] Mark: One more: cache invalidation — if we change prompts or policies, how quickly does prefix cache evict?
[10:18] Priya: Cache TTLs are configurable; you can purge keys when you roll prompts. We also version prompts to avoid accidental collisions.

[10:32] Jordan: Ok I'm going to run through a worked example with your numbers. You said bursts to 45 qps and avg 600 tokens — for a conservative pilot assume 20% cache hit and 30% batching efficiency — that reduces effective tokens by roughly 44% combined (approx). So your 4.16B tokens estimate might become ~2.3B tokens effective. At hosted blended rate of $0.01/1k that's $23k/month — right around your 25k target. If we can boost cache hit to 35% and increase batching efficiency to 40% with Dedicated you might hit $15k/month effective.
[11:12] Emily: Those conversion assumptions are helpful to see. We'll need the benchmarking spreadsheet.
[11:18] Priya: We'll send our benchmarking workbook — it includes sample sims for batching windows, seq length histograms, KV hit rate inputs and modeled per-token equivalent.

[11:40] Mark: What about cold-start and scaling behavior for Dedicated — if we have sudden spikes, will Redwood autoscale or do we overprovision?
[11:47] Priya: Dedicated has autoscaling policies and burst capacity options; you can set buffer pools for spikes. There's an SLA tradeoff — if you need instant scaling to very high QPS without pre-warmed capacity, hosted may absorb spikes better.

[12:07] Jordan: Quick objection handling — if someone says "we achieved lower cost with vendor X", we ask for the same workload details and utilization to compare. Some vendors appear cheaper per-token but don't include infra, routing, or they use lower-quality model variants which may not meet accuracy bar.

[12:26] Emily: We might run two model classes: small for routine tasks, large for reasoning. Can Redwood route and manage rollouts?
[12:33] Jordan: Yes, rollouts and route policies supported. You can A/B between models or do canary on a subset.

[12:45] Samantha: Anything around monitoring cost anomalies?
[12:49] Priya: We have cost alerts per route and token-level traces; you can also export to your own metrics.

[13:03] Mark: I have one nit: your per-1k token numbers earlier sounded high relative to our prior invoices; are discounts automatic or negotiated?
[13:11] Jordan: Discounts are negotiated for committed spend and pilot terms. We'll show list vs typical enterprise discount bands in the pricing sheet.

[13:30] 
-- mid call: more whiteboard-style back-and-forth, some mis-transcriptions --
[21:02] Priya: ...and on quantization: a 4-bit or 8-bit quant can change memory footprint; for some model architectures you need calibration. We'll include notes in the bench sheet.

[22:18] Emily: For evaluation, we want to test at 8k and 16k sequences for a subset; where does batching behave differently at those lengths?
[22:26] Priya: Longer sequences increase memory pressure; batching becomes constrained because KV cache memory balloons. That can reduce batch sizes. Our kernel selector tries to choose optimized kernels for long context but cost per token can rise with longer seqs. We'll show per-1k delta at 8k/16k in the spreadsheet.

[25:00] Jordan: Ok wrapping to next steps: Jordan will send pricing and a pilot template, Priya sends benchmarking workbook, customer provides traffic histograms, schedule the deep-dive.
[25:12] Mark: Sounds good. Any final Qs?
[25:16] Emily: Quick ask — can you include examples of Dedicated break-even points in the deck?
[25:20] Priya: Yup we'll include a break-even calculator.

[25:30] Samantha: Also share sample security addendum and SOC 2 report.

[25:34] Jordan: We'll attach security docs.

[25:45] Jordan: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the materials and proposed pilot contract.

[25:51] Mark: Thanks, bye.

Notes: transcription has occasional mis-hearings ("K-V" vs "KV", "V-P-C" vs "VPC"), a few overlaps. Call duration ~48 minutes but transcript excerpts above capture the cost-focused segments.
